- Stifel cut its Credo Technology price target to $250 from $310 on Nov. 20 but kept its Buy rating, and the new target is 150% above Friday’s close.
- Credo is 67% below its June high as Marvell Technology buys Lumentum and MaxLinear goes after Credo’s cable business.
- Astera Labs’ 154% third-quarter revenue growth says AI connectivity demand is holding up, so the question is Credo’s share and optics ramp.

Credo Technology (CRDO) fell 15.2% to $99.86 on Friday, Nov. 20, as chip stocks sold off, leaving it 67% below its June high. The same day, Stifel cut its price target for the second time in seven weeks, to $250 from $310. It kept its Buy rating, and $250 is still 150% above the stock.
Marvell Technology (MRVL) is buying Lumentum to build a bigger optics rival, while Astera Labs (ALAB) just grew third-quarter revenue 154%, a sign AI connectivity demand hasn’t gone anywhere.
Rivals Moved In as Credo’s Bar Went Up
Credo’s Sept. 1 report beat its own guidance, with revenue of $479.0 million, up 115% from a year earlier. But if the second quarter lands at its guidance midpoint, management’s call for more than 85% growth this fiscal year needs over $1.46 billion in the second half, and optics has to carry much of it.
On Oct. 22, MaxLinear’s CEO put Credo’s share of active electrical cables at “93% or maybe 99%,” and said MaxLinear sees 20% to 30% of the 1.6T cable market within a couple of years, selling chips to cable makers for one or two large U.S. data centers. On Nov. 2, Marvell agreed to buy Lumentum in an all-stock deal.
How Stifel Gets to $250
Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg expects a “beat and raise” on Dec. 1, on cable strength and optics execution, according to TheFly. The firm tied the cut to multiple compression across the chip industry.
Here’s our math: $250 is 26x the $9.71 of normalized EPS analysts expect in fiscal 2028, up from $9.08 90 days ago. The stock trades at 10x that same number today.
Does $250 Add Up?
The Street’s average target has climbed over the past year, from $163 to $277.
TD Cowen’s $175, cut from $300 on Nov. 16 with its Buy kept, matches the Street’s lowest target.
At about 14x the $7.30 analysts expect over the next 12 months, Credo trades below its Nov. 5 low of 15x, against a 3-year average of 61x.
If Credo’s quarterly earnings keep growing, $250 a year from now would be under 26x forward earnings. That’s below where Credo traded on Sept. 30 (27x), and below Astera Labs’ 31x on Nov. 19.

There are moments on the trail when Karen Sparks stops running. She puts her hands to her knees, opens her mouth, and lets the sound that’s been building find release. The noise starts low and feral, then rises from the depths, growing sharp and loud enough to echo under the canopy of oaks where she runs each day. Karen doesn’t care who hears it. The sound fuels her.
Karen took up running in the years after she lost her world. She liked the feel of her feet pounding the earth; the shock and adrenaline needed somewhere to go. But it wasn’t until she discovered this wooded trail in Erwin Park in McKinney, Texas, that she felt something close to peace. Nature is her church. She was raised Baptist but can no longer bring herself to enter a church. She’s been angry with God.
Erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape. Tucked away inside the trees, Karen feels protected. She talks to her kids. She talks to herself. She runs along the dry-cracked mud, next to riverbeds and over trees fallen in the path.
Karen strained her piriformis, a buttock muscle, when she was younger. She’s 43 now, and sometimes when she’s running her hamstrings get so tight it feels like her muscles might rip. Maybe she likes being in pain, or maybe she likes knowing that the pain does not own her. Anyway, she’s in pain all the time. Spiritually, emotionally, physically. When it gets bad, she tries talking to her body. I’m grateful for this hamstring, she says. I’m grateful for this pain. She thinks about people who can’t do this. Because they’re in a wheelchair or in a hospital bed, or because they’re not here anymore.
She thinks about Reagan and Grant.
On the fifth anniversary of their death, November 1, 2015, she ran a hundred miles on the nine-mile loop in Erwin Park. She’d originally signed up for the Indiana Trail 100, but the pandemic brought an end to that plan, and Karen could not be deterred. So she created her own race, an ultramarathon for one. People told her she was crazy, and maybe she was. But she’d spent previous anniversaries hiding from the world, walloped by grief, and this year she was flipping the script on the tragedy that had come to define her life.
The trail was steep and winding. After sunset, the moon lit her path. Each time she thought about quitting, her mind flashed to the man who took her children. Each step was vengeance. Her feet pounded and pounded, like she could pound him into the ground.
On the day her children died, Karen could not move. She remembers falling to the floor in the living room of her parents’ house, curling her body around a framed picture of Reagan and Grant that she clutched to her chest. A neighbor had phoned to say the home she once shared with the man she no longer called her husband was burning, and she dialed her father, who was on his way to pick up the kids.
He’s killing my kids, she said, and she kept repeating the words, because some dark force had overtaken her, and it’s like she knew. Dad, hurry. He’s killing them.
Her father dashed to the scene, where he found firefighters and a home lapped by flames. Karen stayed frozen, and she still gets angry when she thinks of this detail. Why didn’t she go to them? When temperatures rise, running performance tends to drop. Both the research and anyone who’s put in miles on a hot summer afternoon can confidently tell you that much.
But what about when the mercury moves in the opposite direction? Does colder weather in the winter—ranging from just a bit chilly to downright frigid—take a toll on your running too?
A recent review published in Temperature suggests it does. According to the study’s authors, when our muscles get too cold, neuromuscular function becomes impaired. On the run, this can contribute to stiffness, less power output, and decreased endurance, all of which may cause your winter workouts to feel harder than usual.
The good news? You can still run strong when the temps drop—as long as you make a few key training adjustments before, during, and after you log your miles in the colder months of the year. Here’s how to do just that.
How Cold Does It Have to Be to Affect Performance?
There’s no exact number on the thermometer at which runners can universally expect their power, speed, or endurance to decline, Stephen Cheung, PhD, the lead author of the aforementioned review, tells Runner’s World.
Temperature is just one of the many factors that contribute to how well we perform in the cold, Cheung explains. “It’s a function of the environment, as well as how much heat you’re generating, the speed that you’re moving at, and of course, the amount of clothing that you’re wearing,” he says.
Each of these factors varies significantly from runner to runner and affects how quickly their bodies lose heat. You only need to consider those in your run group who run shirtless when it’s freezing versus those who bundle up when it’s 50 degrees Fahrenheit to understand that we all thermoregulate (maintain our internal body temperature) differently. And the equation only becomes more complex when you account for wind and moisture—both in the environment and what you create yourself from air resistance and sweat.
Heather Milton, CSCS, lead exercise physiologist at Primary MD and cofounder of Master My Run, agrees. “It would be great to be able to say, when the temperature outside reaches [a certain point], your pace slows down by this many seconds per mile—but that’s not how it works,” she says.
Keeping this in mind, Milton says the cleanest reference point for runners to begin paying more attention to how they prepare for runs in the cold is when the temperature drops below freezing. Generally speaking, the colder it gets from there, the more noticeable the negative effects on performance will be, she explains.
How Do Cold Temperatures Affect Running?
Cold weather leads to vasoconstriction, Milton explains, which means our blood vessels constrict more, so the muscles farther away from the core don’t receive as much blood flow. If your fingers or toes have ever gone numb in the cold, for example, you’ve experienced the joy of vasoconstriction. Our bodies prioritize heating our core over our extremities because it helps our vital organs maintain a consistent temperature, which is essential for survival in dangerous conditions.
This physiological response, however, doesn’t bode especially well for running performance.

A Fresh AI Position While Alphabet Was Trimmed
During the quarter, Appaloosa cut its Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) Class C stake by 45.9%, from 1,850,000 shares to 1,000,000. Appaloosa was one of 9 buyers among 13 tracked institutional investors, and the only new position in that group. The quarter-end value works out to roughly $137.30 per share. Oracle traded at $152.94 when it reported earnings on September 10, 2026.
A $664 Billion Backlog Anchors the Thesis
Oracle’s fiscal first-quarter revenue came in at $19.34B[3], up 29.6% YoY and ahead of the $19.13B consensus. Cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121%[3] to $7.39B. Remaining performance obligations, meaning signed revenue Oracle has not yet recognized, hit $664B[3], up $209B YoY. Management raised fiscal 2027 guidance to at least $90B[3] in revenue and non-GAAP EPS of $8.10.
Pricing power backs up that demand. GPU utilization reached 97.9%[4], and capacity up for renewal was re-signed at a 20% premium. Cloud infrastructure executive Clay Magouyrk said, “Customer demand continues to support this investment.”[4]
That growth carries a steep price tag. Quarterly capex was $28.5B[3], leaving free cash flow at -$5.4B, after -$23.7B for fiscal 2026. Non-current debt stood at $117.7B as of the fiscal third quarter, and Oracle completed a $20 billion equity program to help fund the expansion. Management has given no specific timeline for a return to positive free cash flow. All of that capex has to be powered, cooled, and connected by somebody, and we covered seven suppliers riding the same data-center expansion in a free AI infrastructure report.
What a 13F Leaves Out for Retirement Investors

This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A hypothetical 61-year-old retiree has $420,000 of Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO | AVGO Price Prediction) stock inside her 401(k). She files single, she is past 59½, and her plan offers a straight rollover of the whole account into an IRA.
The stock fell 11% on Friday after analyst Ming-Chi Kuo posted that Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) unit Google cut its 2027 TPU 8i shipments by about 1M units.
Taking that rollover could cost her more than $30,000. Her shares carry an illustrative cost basis of $70,000, which leaves $350,000 of gain that built up inside the plan. If she rolls the shares into an IRA, every dollar of that gain will be taxed as ordinary income when she withdraws it.
One Rollover Form Erases Her Capital Gains Rate
IRS Publication 575 shows how this works. In its example, a plan participant sells stock distributed from his plan and rolls the $60,000 of proceeds into an IRA, and “the entire $60,000 rolled over will be ordinary income when he withdraws it from his IRA.”
She has another option. Under 26 U.S.C. § 402(e)(4)(B)[1], net unrealized appreciation (NUA) in employer shares received as part of a lump-sum distribution is left out of her gross income. She pays ordinary income tax on the basis now. The appreciation is taxed later at capital gains rates, when she sells.
A poster on the Bogleheads forum who was considering the same move laid out the steps. Open a taxable brokerage account and a rollover IRA, then ask the 401(k) custodian for a lump-sum distribution. The shares go to the brokerage account and everything else goes to the IRA.
Running Her Numbers: $100,800 Versus $69,300
Assume her IRA withdrawals land in the 24% bracket. For single filers in 2026, that bracket covers taxable income from $105,700 to $201,775.
Taking the full stock value out of an IRA at that rate costs about $100,800 in federal tax.
Under NUA, she owes 24% on the basis now, which is $16,800. When she sells, the gain is taxed at 15%. Single filers stay at that rate until taxable income tops $545,500.
That’s a $31,500 difference. It increases if her IRA withdrawals end up taxed above 24%.
Friday’s Drop Makes the Case for Selling Early
NUA also gives her a way out of a concentrated position. She can sell the shares soon after the distribution and diversify, paying capital gains rates on the NUA. Kuo put the shipment cut at roughly 20% of Google’s planned TPU 8i shipments. That shows how much one customer decision can move a single stock.

It made up 18.49% of a $5.05 billion reported portfolio. The filing lists 3.74 million shares worth about $933 million as of September 30. Baupost held its Amazon share count flat during the quarter.
How Amazon’s Portfolio Weight Rose Without a Purchase
Amazon’s weight rose from 16.48% in the June filing to 18.49% at the end of September, with the share count flat. A holding’s weight rises when it outperforms the rest of the book or when other positions shrink.
The filing clearly shows the second effect. Baupost cut its share counts in Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) and Union Pacific (NYSE:UNP) by more than 30% each. It also opened a new stake in Honeywell Aerospace (NASDAQ:HONA): 1.13 million shares worth about $175 million.
The filing shows a value investor who trimmed elsewhere and left his top position alone. Alphabet still sits at 6.41% of the portfolio and Union Pacific at 4.29%.
What Klarman Appears to See in AWS
Klarman built his reputation on buying with a margin of safety, so a stock trading near 25 times forward earnings as his top holding stands out. Amazon Web Services revenue grew 39%[1] year over year in the third quarter to $45.98 billion, its fastest pace in about five years.
AWS operating income reached $17.77 billion[1] versus $11.43 billion a year earlier, and consolidated operating income rose 61%. CEO Andy Jassy said “AWS investment is working”[1] and pointed to projected AWS growth “of over 40% both in 2027 and in 2028.”
That growth comes with a steep bill. Amazon plans roughly $220 billion[1] in capital spending for fiscal 2026, and trailing free cash burn sits near $42.4 billion.
Third-quarter GAAP EPS of $1.89[1] also came in below the $1.96 consensus. Sitting tight through all that suggests Baupost is valuing AWS earnings power several years out and accepting thin cash flow in the meantime.
What Retirement Investors Can Learn From Klarman’s Amazon Stake
Keep in mind that 13F data is outdated by design, as positions are reported roughly 45 days after quarter-end, and Amazon has moved since. Shares closed at $246.82 on November 20, down 7.44% over the past week but still up 6.93% year to date.
Position sizing is the bigger lesson here. Most investors trim a winner the moment it gets big, but Klarman let Amazon run to nearly a fifth of his reported portfolio while cutting other large positions.
For a retirement account, though, an 18% single-stock weight is aggressive, and a 13F only captures part of what Baupost manages. Investors studying the thesis can weigh it against their own risk tolerance and concentration limits.
Our Verdict on Klarman’s Amazon Conviction
Klarman’s Amazon position is worth following as a research signal, because it rests on measurable AWS acceleration and a willingness to wait. The test for anyone studying it is whether the $220 billion[1] expansion turns into the 40%-plus AWS growth Jassy projected.
If that happens, Baupost’s patience will look smart. If capex keeps exceeding cash flow, the margin of safety gets thinner.

But it is worth noting the aspect of the Cardinals’ roster that took a step back from 2025 to ‘26: the bullpen. Cardinals relievers put up a 4.40 ERA in 2026 (20th in MLB), which was roughly three-quarters of a run worse than the 3.74 they put up in 2025 (10th), and for that matter the 3.64 they notched in 2024 (seventh). In the past decade, only the 4.47 ERA of 2023 (23rd) was worse for the franchise.
Now, the Cardinals are in many ways focusing on compiling as much pitching as possible moving forward, to the point that it’s a signature plank of everything president of baseball operations Chaim Bloom and his staff are doing. But in the short term, St. Louis does need to see improvement from its bullpen. It’s tough for a young team to build up its confidence if its bullpen keeps giving up leads in the late innings. (The 2026 Cardinals tied for MLB’s third-most blown saves, with 30, and sixth-most relief losses, with 34).
So what does the Cardinals’ bullpen look like for 2027? Here are four key questions facing Bloom and company this offseason:
Whither Riley O’Brien?
In some ways, 2026 was a great season for O’Brien. He tied the great Mason Miller for the National League lead in saves with 38. He made the NL All-Star team. He even had a pretty cool entrance video at Busch Stadium. It’s all very impressive for a guy who, before 2025, was 30 years old and had thrown exactly 10 1/3 big league innings.
But it’s undeniable that O’Brien fell off as the season went along. He was a miserable 0-6 with a 5.11 ERA in the second half, and his walk rate nearly doubled after the break. He looked like a superstar in April; he looked pedestrian after that. O’Brien is still under team control for four more seasons – he’s 31 and still hasn’t hit arbitration yet – so the Cardinals are in no hurry to give up on him. But it seems unlikely he’ll just be handed the closer role on Opening Day, either.

The Cardinals might be more excited about Gastelum than any other young pitcher on the roster, and if there’s a likely candidate to battle O’Brien for the closer spot, it would have to be him. CHARLESTON, S.C., Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Palmetto Publishing has released A Change of Scenery, a travel memoir and photography collection by Jeff Stern. The book traces a journey through all seven continents, beginning with a solo trip to the American Southwest in March 2020 after a photography conference was cancelled and much of the world stopped moving.
Stern structures the book continent by continent. Each photograph appears alongside the full sensory record of the moment it was made. Readers encounter the smoky, fermented taste of kymyz offered inside a Kyrgyz yurt, frost crystals falling as a tent unzips on the Sary-Jaz Mountains at sunrise, and robusta coffee two hours after dawn in the rice paddies of Northwest Vietnam. At White Pocket in Arizona, standing on rock that pulsed terracotta and ochre beneath a cobalt sky, Stern made himself a promise about the role creative expression would play in the rest of his life.
The book's central tension is one of self-definition. Stern resists the label of landscape photographer, describing it as a box that felt polished, precise, and oddly impersonal. He calls himself a scenery enthusiast instead, arguing that scenery is not a view but a sensory event. That renaming required him to set aside the technical measures by which photographers are usually judged and to trust a creative voice he spent much of his life believing he did not have.

Insurers hoping to sue contractors in subrogation over construction defects are strictly bound by North Carolina’s six-year statute of repose—which starts at occupancy, even if some repairs were made years after a structure was completed, the state’s Court of Appeals said last week.
“Allowing the statute of repose to toll or start running anew each time a repair is made would subject a defendant to potential open-ended liability for an indefinite period of time, defeating the very purpose of statutes of repose,” the appeals court wrote in Holton vs. Valuebuild Homes et al, quoting from 1999 and 2014 appellate court decisions.
The court explained that Nate and Christine Holton in 2015 contracted with Value Build Homes for construction of a residence in Moore County. A certificate of occupancy was issued on May 17, 2016.
Within weeks, though, part of the kitchen floor began sagging. The contractor’s workers came and stabilized the area. Later, the plaintiff homeowners said the house was never level and had presented defects since they had moved in. In 2023, after consulting another contractor, the couple told the homebuilder that they were concerned that the house had been built on an improperly sloped ground or foundation.
Value Build Homes workers looked at the property in 2024 and took some measurements, the court opinion explained.
It wasn’t until January 2025, more than eight years after the clock on the North Carolina statute of repose had started running, that the homeowners filed suit against the homebuilder, alleging breach of contract, construction defects, and negligence. A trial court judge agreed with the defendant homebuilder and granted summary judgment, effectively dismissing the lawsuit.
The Holtons appealed, arguing that the 2024 visit by the builder should have restarted the statute of repose clock, allowing the lawsuit to continue. North Carolina’s repose statute reads: ” …a plaintiff has the burden of showing that he or she brought the action within six years of either (1) the substantial completion of the house or (2) the specific last act or omission of defendant giving rise to the cause of action.”
But the Court of Appeals, in the opinion written by Judge Allegra Collins, emphasized the first part of that law. Previous court rulings have held that a building is substantially complete when certificate of occupancy is issued. A simple repair does not qualify as a “last act” under the statute, the opinion found, citing other court decisions.
The evidence “shows that defendants investigated plaintiffs’ complaints in 2024 by excavating near the foundation and taking measurements. Investigative activities of this nature do not constitute construction work or repairs extending the statutory repose period,” Judge Collins wrote.
And because the plaintiffs had stated that “the house was never level since day 1,” that showed that the homeowners knew early on about the problem and could have sued before the six-year window closed. “Unlike a wholly latent condition, the condition forming the basis of plaintiffs’ claims was apparent in 2016,” the court said.

The software giant's shares have dropped after six of its past 10 December reports. Does this year's setup look any different?

Key Points
- Adobe hosts its fiscal fourth-quarter earnings call after the close on Wednesday, Dec. 9.
- Adobe shares dropped in reaction to six of the company's last 10 fiscal fourth-quarter reports.
- The stock trades at around 9 times what Adobe earned on an adjusted basis in its past four quarters.
Adobe (ADBE +0.94%) stock has fallen in reaction to six of the company's last 10 December earnings reports. And the drops have been far bigger than the gains. None of the four up days topped 4%, while four of the six down days were worse than 6%, including a nearly 14% dive in December 2024.
The creative software company will hold its next earnings call after the close on Wednesday, Dec. 9.
But the stock heads into this one in a much different place. Shares closed at around $222 on Nov. 19, down about 37% so far this year, and trade at about 9 times what Adobe earned on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis in its last four quarters.
The stock didn't go into any of those 10 reports this cheap. And I think the price matters more than the track record.
Image source: Getty Images.
Six drops and four gains
Adobe normally posts results after the close and hosts its call at 2 p.m. Pacific time, so the reaction comes the next trading day. In 2020 and 2021, it reported before the open and held a meeting with financial analysts, so those rows use the same day's move.
The last column divides the stock price at the start of each report by the adjusted earnings per share for the fiscal year the report covers.
The four gains averaged less than 3%. The six drops averaged almost 7%.
What drives the stock on report day?
In recent years, the December report is also where Adobe lays out its targets for the next fiscal year. And those targets seem to matter more to the stock than the quarter itself.
Showing how much the outlook can weigh on shares, Adobe ended fiscal 2024 with revenue of $21.5 billion, up 11%, and its fiscal 2025 target called for $23.30 billion to $23.55 billion. That worked out to growth of about 9% at the midpoint. The stock sank almost 14% the next day.

Missouri’s budget crisis didn’t come out of nowhere
Years of tax cuts, rising spending and dwindling reserves have left Missouri facing billions in potential budget reductions.
Missouri Gov. Mike Parson during his State of the State address on Jan. 19, 2022 (Tim Bommel/Missouri House Communications).
Nearly a decade ago, then-Auditor Nicole Galloway issued a stark warning.
Her February 2018 budget stress test found Missouri increasingly dependent on individual income taxes and ill-equipped to weather an economic downturn.
“If there are economic bumps in the road ahead,” she said, “our state is not prepared.”
The report got a round of news stories. Then everyone moved on. Five months later, then-Gov. Mike Parson signed legislation touted as the largest single-year income tax cut in Missouri history.
Flash forward to last week, when a task force studying Missouri’s public school funding formula was told the legislature will likely need to cut $1.5 billion to $3.5 billion from what state agencies want to spend next year.
Missouri faces nearly $3 billion gap between spending requests and tax revenue
So what happened between the warnings and public discussion of a multibillion-dollar budget hole?
Federal pandemic assistance and unexpectedly strong tax collections helped Missouri build a massive surplus. By June 2023, the state’s general revenue fund held approximately $5.8 billion.
That gave lawmakers room to invest, increase spending and cut taxes.
So they did all three.
In 2022, Parson signed another income tax cut he called the largest in state history, estimated to reduce annual revenue by $764 million. A year later, lawmakers eliminated state income taxes on Social Security and public pension payments, at an estimated cost of $309 million a year.
Then, in 2025, Gov. Mike Kehoe signed legislation eliminating the state income tax on capital gains — profits from selling investments.
Originally estimated to cost $111 million annually, the exemption proved considerably more expensive. Its impact on fiscal 2026 revenue was later estimated at more than $500 million.
Meanwhile, spending grew.
Galloway’s successor, State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick, documented just how quickly. From fiscal 2020 to 2025, general revenue grew 45.8%, while spending increased 53.4%. Inflation over that period was 24.5%.
Not all that spending growth was discretionary. Medicaid costs increased, pandemic assistance expired and maintaining existing programs became more expensive.
Nor is every appropriated dollar spent. Agencies leave money unused because of vacancies and project delays.
Still, Missouri was authorizing more spending than it collected annually and relying on the surplus to cover the difference. Now the money that made those budgets possible is nearly gone.
In December 2025, Fitzpatrick warned that continued deficit spending could exhaust the general revenue fund by fiscal year 2028. He repeated the warning in June, after lawmakers approved another budget exceeding projected revenue.

According to prosecutors, between 2016 and 2017, Said Yahyapour, of Stratham, obtained money from various financial institutions that was to be used to make payments to Portfolio Holding, Inc. in order to fund extended warranty contracts and insurance policies he sold customers of his dealership in Somersworth. A jury found that Yahyapour kept the money to fund other obligations of the dealership instead of paying Portfolio to ensure the customers received the coverage he sold to them.
Attorney General John M. Formella said that Yahyapour was sentenced in Strafford Superior Court following his conviction on September 24, 2026 by a Strafford County Superior Court jury of 32 counts of theft.

The FBI is investigating a suspected breach of a nationwide database used by federal, state and local law enforcement agencies to share criminal justice information, CNN reported on Nov. 20, citing two people briefed on the investigation.
The apparent compromise of the National Crime Information Center database would mark the second intrusion involving an FBI system in recent months and the latest in a string of cyber incidents that have alarmed US officials over the past week.
The agency did not respond to a request for comment from Reuters.
The FBI database is used by law enforcement agencies nationwide to store and share information on warrants, criminal histories and background checks.
Previous high-profile cyber disruptions over the past week have included a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights.
A September breach by a digital extortion group known as “ShinyHunters” accessed an FBI jobs website, compromising data on current and former FBI employees.
